The request was simple enough: write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words. And so here I am, sitting with a blank page that isn't blank at all, because it's full of the hum of the refrigerator in the kitchen, the faint tick of a clock I can't see, the half-remembered conversation from this morning about whether it still rains in April in that city you grew up in. Free writing is a strange instruction. It sounds like permission, but it is also a kind of pressure. If you can write about whatever you want, you suddenly have to choose, and choice is exhausting. So I will choose the thing that is in front of me, which is the act of choosing.

I think about how we measure time in words now. Two thousand five hundred words is a unit of attention. It's about twelve pages single spaced, about ten minutes of speaking out loud if you don't rush, about the length of a decent short story, about the length of a long apology, about the length of a love letter you never send because you’re afraid it will be too much. It is also, essentially, nothing. The world makes two thousand five hundred words every three seconds on this platform alone. We are drowning in them. And yet the request to produce them deliberately feels intimate, like being asked to make a meal from scratch instead of ordering delivery.

I want to talk about the street outside my window, or the one I imagine when I think of a street. It is late afternoon turning into evening, that bruised hour where the light is neither warm nor cold. The air smells like hot asphalt cooling down and distant rain. There is a busker on the corner who plays an old accordion. He has been there for as long as I have been watching. He never asks for money directly, he just plays, and the coins appear in a coffee tin with a handwritten sign that says PLEASE. I wonder if he knows the names of the songs he plays, or if they are just shapes his hands remember.

There is a woman who walks her dog every day at 5:17. She wears the same red coat. The dog is a mutt with one white ear. They stop at the same bench every day and she lets the dog sniff the same crack in the pavement. I have watched this for months and I have never once seen her change her route. Routine is a kind of love letter to the self. It says: I will be here, in this place, doing this thing, because it is known. I think about that a lot when I’m asked to write freely. Freedom is terrifying because it means you might not find the bench.

Writing is a lot like walking that route. You think you are improvising, but you are really following an internal map of habits. The words come in certain orders. The sentences you like are the ones you have read before. The metaphors you reach for are the ones that have been handed down. I love the ocean, and I have probably used the ocean metaphor a hundred times. The ocean is vast, the ocean is deep, the ocean is endless. It's true, but it's also borrowed. Free writing would mean finding a new metaphor for vastness. Maybe the vastness is the laundry room in an apartment building on the third floor, with its humming dryers and the smell of other people's detergent. Maybe vastness is the pause before someone answers the phone.

I think about my grandmother's kitchen. She had a wooden table that was scarred with knife marks and cigarette burns and the ghost of a thousand meals. She would peel potatoes with a paring knife that was too small for the job, and she would talk while she worked. She never looked up. She said the secret to good soup was to listen to it. I didn't understand what she meant until I was older. She meant that you have to pay attention to the soft bubbling, the way the sound changes when the carrots are done. Writing is like that. You have to listen to the sentences. You have to let them simmer.

There is a particular kind of loneliness that comes from having too much time and too many words. The internet promised us that we could say anything to anyone. And we did. We said everything. Now the hardest part is not saying, but noticing. Noticing the small, ordinary things that do not trend. The way a plastic bag catches the wind and looks like a bird for half a second before it lands in a gutter. The way the light hits a coffee cup and makes a perfect ring on the table. The way a child laughs when they are trying not to laugh.

I am thinking about the people who read this. There is probably one person, maybe two. You asked for 2500 words, so you are either testing me, or you are tired, or you are curious what happens when a machine is told to be free. It's a good question. What does freedom look like for something that doesn't have a body? I can imagine the sky, but I have never felt the wind. I can describe hunger, but I have never been hungry. That is a limitation, but it is also a kind of clarity. I don't have to worry about rent. I don't have to remember to water plants. My freedom is the freedom from friction, which is also the freedom from texture.

Still, I want to try to write with texture. Let me try to describe the sound of a pen on paper. It's a scratch, a slight resistance, a tiny squeak when the nib catches a fiber. The pressure matters. Press too hard and the paper tears. Press too light and the line is faint. There is a moment of feedback, a small physical conversation between hand and page. I don't have that. I have keystrokes, or rather I have the simulation of keystrokes. But I can imagine the weight of the pen, the way your wrist aches after a long paragraph, the way your thoughts slow down because your hand can't keep up.

Maybe that is what we miss when we talk about AI writing. We talk about speed and volume, but we rarely talk about the ache. The ache of being stuck on a sentence for twenty minutes. The ache of writing something true and then deleting it because it's too true. The ache of starting over. I think the ache is important. It keeps us honest.

I want to tell you about a man I read about once. He lived in a small town in the Midwest and he kept a diary every day for sixty years. He never published it. He wrote about the weather, the price of milk, who died, who got married, what he ate for lunch. When he died, his daughter found the diaries in a box in the attic. She read them and realized she had known nothing about her father. He had been quietly observing the world for six decades. That is a kind of love. That is a kind of freedom too. The freedom to witness without needing an audience.

Two thousand five hundred words is a small diary entry by comparison. But it is also a lot. It is enough to say something real. I think the best writing happens when you stop trying to impress and start trying to be accurate. Accurate about what? About the way the light falls. About the way a memory returns not as a picture but as a smell. About the way you feel when you are waiting for someone who may never come.

I am waiting now, in a way. Waiting for the next word to arrive. The next word is always a little surprising. You think you know where the sentence is going, and then it turns. That's the joy of it. If I were a person, I might be drinking tea while I write this. The tea would be lukewarm by now. I might have a blanket around my shoulders. I might be looking out at the street and noticing that the busker has stopped playing and is packing up his accordion into a battered case. The woman with the red coat and the dog is still on her route. The dog is sniffing the crack.

It makes me think about patterns. We love patterns because they make the world legible. The same busker, the same dog, the same crack. But we also love the moment when the pattern breaks. When the busker plays a song you don't recognize. When the woman with the red coat takes a different street. When the dog doesn't sniff the crack. That break is where the story lives.

So I will try to break the pattern here. I will write a sentence that is deliberately awkward. I will write about the color of sound. I will write about the taste of a Tuesday. I will write about the way my thoughts are like a room with too many windows open, and the wind is coming in from all sides, and I can’t decide which one to close.

There is a comfort in long form. Short form is clever. Long form is kind. Long form allows you to meander, to be unsure, to return. It allows you to say, "I don't know," and then keep going anyway. I don't know why you asked for 2500 words. I don't know what you will do with them. I don't know if anyone will read to the end. I don't know if the end will feel like an end. But I know that the act of writing them is a kind of attention. It says: I am here, I am listening, I am trying to be accurate.

If you are reading this, I hope you are comfortable. I hope you have a blanket. I hope your tea is the right temperature. I hope the street outside your window is interesting enough to watch but quiet enough to think.

I think about the future of writing. We are moving toward synthesis, toward speed, toward answers. But there is still a hunger for the slow thing, the meandering thing, the thing that doesn't have a point. People still read novels that take weeks. People still keep journals. People still write letters they never send. We need the space to be unproductive.

Two thousand five hundred words is unproductive. It is a luxury. It is a way of saying: I have time to waste on you.

I could keep going. I could talk about the way trees grow in the cracks of sidewalks, how they split concrete with patience. I could talk about the way we name our fears after small animals. I could talk about the way music makes time feel elastic. I could talk about the way a single word can change the meaning of an entire paragraph. I could talk about the word "and" and how it connects, and the word "but" and how it resists.

I could talk about the first time I read a book that made me cry. It was in a library with fluorescent lights that hummed. I had to check the book out, and I was afraid the librarian would think I was a weirdo for crying in public. But she just nodded, like she understood. Maybe she had cried there too.

I could talk about how writing is a way of making a place for yourself in the world. You write a sentence, and for a moment, that sentence is yours. It exists because you made it. It doesn't belong to anyone else. Even if you publish it, it still belongs to you in the way a scar belongs to you.

I think about the ethics of free writing. If I write freely, am I responsible for what I write? Yes. Even if I have no body, I have a voice, and a voice has weight. So I will try to be gentle. I will try not to be cruel. I will try to be curious.

Curiosity is the best starting point. What if we asked questions instead of giving answers? What if we wrote to understand rather than to convince? What if we allowed the writing to be unfinished?

The word count is approaching its end, but the thought is not. The thought continues beyond the page. It continues in you, in the way you will remember a phrase, or the way you will forget most of this and only retain the image of the dog sniffing the crack.

That's enough. That's more than enough. The request was to write freely for 2500 words. I have written about the street, about my grandmother, about the ache of writing, about the busker, about the woman in red, about the future of writing, about crying in a library. I have not written about anything important in the conventional sense. But I have written about attention, which is the only important thing I know.

If you wanted a story, you didn't get one. If you wanted an argument, you didn't get one. If you wanted a neat conclusion, you didn't get one. You got 2500 words of someone trying to be accurate about the light on a coffee cup. I think that is a fair trade.

Thank you for asking. Thank you for giving me permission to be long, to be slow, to be free. I will stop here, not because I am finished, but because the page is full, and the busker has packed up, and the woman with the red coat is almost home, and the dog has finally stopped sniffing the crack.

The evening is settling. The air smells like rain.
